A lockfile that has not been rebuilt since it was
committed, and a Dockerfile that has not been rebuilt
since it was written, are untested claims. By the end of
this chapter you will be able to look at a green build
and say exactly what it has shown: which of three
automated gates ran, what each one would have caught had
it been absent, and what a missing baseline test still
lets through unnoticed when every gate is green. You will
also know how to turn each gate red on purpose, because a
check that has never been seen to fail has not been shown
to work.

## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 50 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** Chapter 11 (@sec-testing) supplies
`tinytest`, the four kinds of test, and the baseline test
this chapter's verification gate runs. Chapter 3
(@sec-levels) supplies the L0-L3 ladder and the
capture-versus-validation vocabulary this chapter makes
operational. Chapter 6 (@sec-dependencies) supplies the
dependency invariant the dependency-manifest gate
automates, and Chapter 7 (@sec-containers) supplies the
Dockerfile the verify job rebuilds. The R knowledge
assumed is writing and calling a function, together with
enough comfort reading YAML to follow a workflow file
line by line; no YAML is written from scratch here.

**Objectives.** By the end of this chapter, can you:

- explain why a CI runner, carrying none of the author's
  undeclared state, catches a 'works on my machine'
  failure that no test run on the author's own machine
  can?
- name the three automated gates a CI workflow runs,
  state what each one proves, and demonstrate how to make
  each one fail on purpose?
- say why verification (L3) compares computational
  outputs against a committed baseline, within a stated
  tolerance, rather than comparing rendered PDFs or HTML?
- read and extend a checksum manifest that guards the
  integrity of raw input data?
- match the three gates, plus verification, to a
  compendium's archetype, so that a package, a
  manuscript, and a simulation each run only the checks
  appropriate to them?

**Outline.** We begin with the analyst's three
irreplaceable judgments and with where CI sits on the
stack. We then turn to the machine that is not yours, to
the three gates and where their bugs hide, to secrets,
tokens, and pinned actions, and to two CI dialects. The
middle of the chapter treats verification and level L3,
the checksum manifest, the framework's own capture test
matrix, and how CI adapts to five archetypes. We then
consider independent external verification, a worked
example, debugging a failed reproduction, and a gate
demonstrated on this book's own cohort compendium.
Lastly, we discuss collaborating with an LLM, followed by
exercises, a cheat sheet, and further reading.
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

Continuous integration pins nothing, and @fig-stack-ci
marks that explicitly. The three layers its gates touch
(package versions, analysis code, and input data) are
validated here, not captured, because the lockfile, the
scripts, and the raw extract were already pinned or
written by the chapters that came before. This chapter's
whole contribution is confirming, on a machine that is
not the author's, that those captures still hold.

## Orientation

Consider a registry study whose analysis is finished,
whose manuscript is written, and whose lockfile and
container recipe are committed to version control. The
author has done, to all appearances, everything this
book has asked. The packages are pinned (@sec-dependencies),
the environment is fixed in an image (@sec-containers),
the report is literate and regenerates its own figures
(@sec-literate). The compendium sits, by the author's
account, at level L2, a pinned environment. But how
does the author know that the captured environment
actually rebuilds, on a machine that is not the one
where the work was done? Until something tests it, the
author does not know.
A lockfile can reference a package version that has
been pulled from its repository. A Dockerfile can
depend on a base image whose digest has drifted. A
script can silently rely on a file that lives only in
the author's home directory and was never committed.
None of these announce themselves on the machine where
the work already runs, because on that machine the
missing piece is present.

In this chapter we take up the instrument that closes
the gap between a reproducibility claim and its
demonstration. Continuous integration, abbreviated CI,
is a service that rebuilds the
compendium from its committed inputs on every change.
It works in a fresh environment that carries none of
the developer's accumulated and undeclared state, and
runs a battery of checks against the result. We shall see
that CI captures no new layer of the determinant stack.
Its whole contribution is to *validate* that the layers
already captured actually suffice. The distinction between
capturing reproducibility and validating it was drawn in
@sec-intro and carried through every chapter. It reaches
its operational form here: pinning is capture, and CI,
together with the verification command it runs, is
validation.

We then take the ladder to its top rung. Verification,
the L2-to-L3 transition, confirms what has been captured
by regenerating the computational outputs. It compares
them, number for number and within a stated tolerance,
against a recorded baseline. The subtlety, which we
shall press, is in what gets compared. We compare a
derived dataset, a fitted model object, or a results
table, and emphatically not the rendered PDF or HTML,
whose bytes carry timestamps and font identifiers that
defeat a naive comparison. We close with the schemes by
which reproducibility is checked from outside the
author's own project entirely, during peer review.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what CI does not know

An author claims their compendium is at level L2 because
a `Dockerfile` is committed and builds on their laptop.
Does a green CI run of that same `Dockerfile` raise the
compendium's level? What, precisely, does the green run
add?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The level is set by what is captured, not by who
rebuilds it, and a CI run captures nothing. Whether the
compendium is at L2 at all depends on what else is
committed: the rungs are cumulative, so a `Dockerfile`
reaches L2 only beside a lockfile, and without one the
compendium is at L0. The green CI run adds assurance
rather than capture. That is, it shows the same `Dockerfile` also
builds on a machine that carries none of the author's
undeclared state, which the laptop build alone cannot
show. A build that only ever succeeds on the author's own
machine is exactly the 'works on my machine' pattern this
chapter opened with.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

Before turning to the machinery, we note what it cannot
do. Continuous integration is highly automated, but
copying a workflow file into a repository and forgetting
it leaves three decisions unmade. They remain the
analyst's, and no tool makes them.

1. **The analyst decides what counts as a correct
   output, and records the baseline.** Verification can
   compare a regenerated result against a recorded one,
   but it cannot know which results matter or what
   tolerance is acceptable. The baseline may be a
   derived dataset, a coefficient table, or a single
   summary statistic. The agreement required may be to
   the last bit or to a stated numerical tolerance. Both
   are scientific choices the analyst must make and
   defend.

2. **The analyst decides which gates the compendium's
   archetype warrants.** A CI workflow can run `R CMD
   check`, a render gate, and a dependency-manifest gate,
   but not every archetype needs all three. An R-package
   archetype has no report to render; a simulation
   archetype may run a reduced pipeline under CI and the
   full one elsewhere. Matching the gates to the
   archetype is the analyst's call. The aim is that CI
   tests what actually needs testing, without imposing a
   render gate on a project that has nothing to render.

3. **The analyst reads a CI failure as evidence.** A red
   build is CI doing its job: it has found, on a clean
   machine, a dependency the author's machine supplied
   silently. The discipline is to treat the failure as a
   true report about the compendium's reproducibility and
   to fix the captured inputs rather than the check.

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Continuous integration (CI).** A hosted service that,
  on every committed change to a repository, checks out
  the code onto a fresh virtual machine, rebuilds the
  project, and runs a defined set of checks, reporting
  success or failure automatically.
- **Workflow.** The file, written in YAML, that tells the
  CI service what to do: which events trigger it, what
  environment to run in, and what commands to execute. On
  GitHub these files live under `.github/workflows/`; on
  GitLab the single file is `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
- **Runner.** The fresh, ephemeral machine (usually a
  virtual machine or a container) on which the CI service
  executes the workflow. It is discarded after the run,
  so nothing persists between runs except what the
  workflow explicitly restores.
- **`R CMD check`.** R's own quality gate for a package,
  which among many checks verifies that every dependency
  declared in `DESCRIPTION` is installed and findable. A
  research compendium built as an R package inherits this
  gate for free, for its package skin only: `analysis/`
  is excluded from the build and never checked.
- **Render gate.** A CI check that re-renders the
  compendium's report (an R Markdown or Quarto document)
  from source and fails the build if the render errors.
- **Dependency-manifest gate.** A CI check that enforces
  the dependency invariant of @sec-dependencies. In its
  strict, R-package form it requires every package the code
  uses to be declared in `DESCRIPTION` and pinned in
  `renv.lock`. A research compendium's `DESCRIPTION`
  declares only the API exported from `R/`, while its
  analysis scripts legitimately draw on packages present
  in `renv.lock` but not in `DESCRIPTION`. For a
  compendium, therefore, the gate enforces the weaker
  inclusion that every package the code uses is pinned in
  `renv.lock`.
- **Verification.** The act of rebuilding the compendium's
  environment from its recipe and re-running the analysis
  in it. The regenerated computational outputs are then
  compared with a committed baseline, within a stated
  tolerance, by means of a baseline test (@sec-testing);
  passing it is what the ladder calls level L3.
- **Checksum.** A short fingerprint, computed from a
  file's or an object's bytes by a hash function such as
  SHA-256, with the property that any change to the input,
  however small, changes the fingerprint. A stored
  checksum lets a later run detect that an input has been
  altered.
- **Forge.** The platform that hosts the repository and
  runs its CI, such as GitHub or GitLab. The forge governs
  where the code lives and which CI dialect the workflow
  is written in; it pins nothing about the computational
  environment.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the analyst's irreplaceable judgments

Name the one of the three analyst judgments that a
workflow file, however carefully written, cannot make for
itself, and say why.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Any of the three qualifies, but the clearest is the
first: deciding what counts as a correct output and
recording the baseline. A workflow can run a comparison
and report its result. However, it has no way to decide
which quantity matters, which outputs to compare, or what
tolerance distinguishes a real change from floating-point
noise. That is a scientific judgment about the analysis,
and the CI configuration cannot make it.
:::
:::

## The machine that is not yours

We begin with the reason a second machine is needed at
all. An analysis reproduces on the machine where it was
written partly because the machine is generous. It
supplies, without being asked, a package installed
months ago and never recorded, or a system library that
some other project needed. It may equally supply a data
file sitting in a home directory, or an environment
variable set once in a shell profile. Every one of these
is undeclared state, and every one of them is invisible
precisely because it is present. The 'works on my machine' report is true: it
describes a machine that happens to carry more than the
compendium declares.

Continuous integration removes the generosity. When a
change is pushed, the CI service provisions a fresh
runner, a virtual machine or container that has just
been created and carries nothing but a clean operating
system. It checks out exactly what is under version
control, no more, and attempts to rebuild the
compendium from those committed inputs alone. If the
analysis depended on anything the author never declared,
the rebuild fails. It fails here, rather than in a
reviewer's hands or a colleague's re-analysis a year on.
The CI machine catches the 'works on my machine' failure
at its source for a reason that is almost tautological:
the CI machine is, by construction, not the author's. It
cannot supply the author's undeclared state because it
does not have it.

Continuous integration does not pin a
package version, fix an operating system, or record a
session option; those are the work of the lockfile and
the container, done before CI runs. What CI adds is the
repeated, adversarial test that the capture already
performed is sufficient. A captured-but-never-retested
compendium suffers a slow decay. In this failure mode a
declared environment silently stops rebuilding as its
external references drift, and no one notices because no
one has tried to rebuild it. CI is the standing test
that would notice. Removing CI from a repository lowers
no level on the ladder; the compendium is exactly as
reconstructable as before. It simply stops being
checked, and becomes trusted rather than tested.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: why the runner is generous nowhere

Explain, in one or two sentences, why a freshly
provisioned CI runner cannot supply the undeclared state
that makes an analysis 'work on my machine', and why this
is close to a tautology rather than a clever design
feature.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The runner cannot supply undeclared state because it has
none to supply: it was created moments ago from a clean
image and has never run anything else. It is almost a
tautology because the property that makes it useful,
carrying nothing of the author's, is simply what 'fresh'
means. No engineering insight is required to make a
runner forget what it never knew.
:::
:::

## What the checks are: the three gates

A CI run on a research compendium executes, in the
general case, three gates. We take them in turn, because
the division of labor among them is exact.

The first is **`R CMD check`**. Because a research
compendium is structured as an R package (@sec-compendium),
it inherits R's own quality gate at no additional cost.
Among its many checks, the one that matters most for
reproducibility is early and simple. It verifies that
every package the code in `R/` uses is declared in
`DESCRIPTION`, and that every declared package is
installed and findable. On a fresh runner this is a real
test, because the runner has only what the lockfile
declared.

Its scope is narrower than it looks. The
check runs on the package that `R CMD build` makes, and a
compendium's `.Rbuildignore` excludes `analysis/`. The
analysis scripts are therefore never parsed, never run,
and never scanned for packages (@sec-compendium).
`R CMD check` validates the package skin, `R/`, the
tests, and `DESCRIPTION`, and nothing else. Within that
scope there is a second trap. An undeclared package used
in `R/` is reported as a WARNING, not an ERROR, so the
gate fails on it only if it is told to fail on warnings.
A workflow that passes `error_on = 'error'` to
`rcmdcheck`, as many hand-written workflows do, lets the
undeclared dependency through with a green build.

The second is the **render gate**. Where the compendium
carries a report, an R Markdown or Quarto document that
regenerates its own figures and tables, the workflow
re-renders it from source on the runner. A render that
errors, because a chunk references an object that no
longer exists or a package that was not restored, fails
the build. Of the three gates it is the one that executes
the analysis code: a report that sources the
scripts under `analysis/`, or calls the functions they
define, runs them on the runner, against the restored
library and nothing else. The render gate is the literate
document's validation counterpart: @sec-literate seals
the prose to the code, and the render gate confirms, on a
clean machine, that the seal holds. It needs the data on
the runner. The cohort this book uses is synthetic and
committed for that reason. Where the real data are
restricted, CI renders against a synthetic stand-in, and
the real render runs inside the environment approved for
the data. Committing the data to turn a red render gate
green is never the fix.

The third is the **dependency-manifest gate**, the
automated form of the dependency invariant developed in
@sec-dependencies. In its strict form, appropriate to the
R-package archetype, the invariant is a double inclusion.
The set of packages the code actually uses must be a
subset of the set declared in `DESCRIPTION`, which must in
turn be a subset of the set pinned in `renv.lock`. A
research compendium is looser. Its `DESCRIPTION` declares
only the API exported from `R/`, while its analysis
scripts legitimately use packages that appear in
`renv.lock` but never in `DESCRIPTION`. For a compendium
the operative invariant is therefore the single inclusion
that every package the code uses is pinned in `renv.lock`,
and the strict `DESCRIPTION`-inclusion gate does not apply.
The gate scans the source for `library()`, `require()`,
and `pkg::fun()` calls. It then reads `DESCRIPTION` and
`renv.lock`, and stops with an error if a used package is
not pinned. Because it reads the analysis scripts, it is
the gate that covers what `R CMD check` cannot see. Its
core needs no special tool; `renv` itself can find the
packages the code uses. The minimal version below scans
only `analysis/`, the part `R CMD check` never reads:

```r
# ci/dependency-gate.R
used <- unique(renv::dependencies('analysis')$Package)
locked <- names(renv::lockfile_read('renv.lock')$Packages)
base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = 'base'))
missing <- setdiff(used, c(locked, base_pkgs))
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  stop('Used in analysis/ but not pinned in renv.lock: ',
       toString(missing))
}
```

A companion tool, `zzrenvcheck`, does the same scan with
more care (tests, vignettes, version constraints, and the
stricter `DESCRIPTION` inclusion for the package
archetype). Its `error_on_fail` argument decides whether
a failed check stops the step with a nonzero exit status
or only prints a report. The default is
`!interactive()`, so a call from `Rscript` already stops,
but CI should pass `error_on_fail = TRUE` explicitly so
that the gate does not depend on how R was started. It is
not on CRAN, so the workflow installs it from its source
repository, pinned to a commit. Either form catches the
most common drift: a package installed interactively
during analysis, used in the code, and never
snapshotted, so that the lockfile is silently
incomplete.

How do the three gates fit together in practice? A
condensed GitHub Actions workflow that runs them on every
push and pull request illustrates the shape of the
thing. It uses the R community's `r-lib/actions` for the
setup and the check, at the major versions current when
this chapter was revised in November 2026
(`actions/checkout@v7`, `r-lib/actions/*@v2`). We show
it as a static file. Its
YAML was checked for syntax, and the command in each gate
was run against a toy compendium. However, the workflow
as a whole is executed by the CI service, never by this
book.

```yaml
name: compendium

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  gates:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    env:
      GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Install the R version recorded in renv.lock.
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: renv
          use-public-rspm: true

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-pandoc@v2

      # Restore renv.lock into the project library. A
      # stock renv .Rprofile activates that library in
      # every later R step run from the repository root.
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2

      # The gate tools are not analysis dependencies, so
      # they are not in renv.lock. zzrenvcheck comes from
      # a personal repository and is pinned to a commit.
      - name: Install the gate tools
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: |
          renv::install(c('rcmdcheck', 'remotes', 'pkgload'))
          remotes::install_github(
            'rgt47/zzrenvcheck',
            ref = '6f53235668cb4048c1ae793d64b10d6505bf69a2')

      # Gate 1: R CMD check of the package skin. Any
      # WARNING, such as an undeclared import, fails.
      - uses: r-lib/actions/check-r-package@v2
        with:
          args: 'c("--no-manual")'
          error-on: '"warning"'

      # Gate 2: every package the code uses, analysis/
      # included, is declared and pinned.
      - name: Dependency-manifest gate
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: |
          zzrenvcheck::check_packages(strict = TRUE,
                                      error_on_fail = TRUE)

      # Gate 3: the report re-renders from source.
      - name: Render gate
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: |
          rmarkdown::render('analysis/report/report.Rmd',
                            output_format = 'html_document',
                            output_dir = tempdir())
```

Three choices in the file merit a word. First, `error-on`
is set to `"warning"` explicitly, although that is also
the action's default. The setting is the whole difference
between a gate that catches an undeclared import and one
that does not. Second, the render gate renders to HTML
into a temporary folder. It tests that every chunk runs,
and leaves PDF typesetting, which needs a LaTeX
installation, to a separate step if the deliverable is a
PDF. Third, nothing in the file is marked
`continue-on-error`; a step that is allowed to fail
without failing the job is a report, not a gate.

The house rule of this book is that a gate is not shown to
work until it has been seen to fail. Each of the three can
be turned red on purpose, in a branch, in a few minutes:

| Gate | Deliberate breakage | What the run reports |
|---|---|---|
| `R CMD check` | Call `sandwich::vcovHC()` in a function in `R/` without adding `sandwich` to `DESCRIPTION` | A WARNING, '`::` or `:::` import not declared from', which `error-on: '"warning"'` turns into a failed step |
| Dependency manifest | Add `library(sandwich)` to a script in `analysis/` without snapshotting | The missing package is listed and the step stops with an error |
| Render | Add a chunk that loads a package absent from `renv.lock`, or uses an object no chunk creates | `rmarkdown::render()` stops at that chunk and names it |

We ran each breakage against a toy compendium (R 4.6.1,
`rcmdcheck` 1.4.0, `zzrenvcheck` from its source
repository in October 2026), and each command exited with a
nonzero status. The first breakage also shows why the
setting matters: with `error_on = 'error'` the same check
returned normally, the WARNING printed and ignored.
Placing `library(sandwich)` in `analysis/` instead of
`R/` shows the scope of the first gate. In that case
`R CMD check` passes and the dependency gate goes red;
the render gate goes red too if the report runs that
script.

### Where CI bugs hide: cross-boundary state

The workflow above takes care over where the pinned
library is restored and from which directory each R step
starts. That care avoids a subtle bug whose cause
generalizes well beyond the particular case.

The trouble is that a CI run is not one continuous
process. It is a sequence of separate steps, each a fresh
shell, and within a step the check itself runs in a
further separate subprocess. State does not automatically
cross these boundaries. In one documented case, the step
that restored the pinned packages installed them
correctly. The very next step, running `R CMD check`,
then reported a required package as 'not available'. The
package was on disk; the check simply could not see where.
Two boundaries conspired. The restore step adjusted the
library path in its own shell, but the next step is a
fresh shell and inherited none of that. And even within
a step, `R CMD check` runs in a child subprocess whose
library path must be passed to it explicitly. Adjusting
the path in the calling session does not propagate to the
child. The fix is to launch the check from a session in
which the restored library is already on the library
path, and to make sure that path travels to the child.

In the workflow above, three pieces combine to do this.
`setup-renv` restores into the project library. Every
later R step starts in the repository root, where the
project's `.Rprofile` activates that library. And
`rcmdcheck()` hands the calling session's `.libPaths()`
to the check subprocess, which is the default of its
`libpath` argument. A workflow that restores into some
other folder must pass that folder to `libpath` by hand.

The second piece is an assumption, and it is the same
cross-boundary bug in waiting. It holds for the stock
`.Rprofile` that `renv::init()` writes, which sources
`renv/activate.R` in every session. It does not hold for
every compendium. The `.Rprofile` that zzcollab
scaffolds activates renv only when `ZZCOLLAB_CONTAINER`
is set to `true`. On a CI host it skips renv, and later steps see
the system library rather than the restored one. Such a
compendium must activate the library explicitly on the
runner: set that variable in the job's environment, or
begin each R step with `source('renv/activate.R')`.

But why did the bug stay hidden? The workflow had passed
for several repositories, because each of them imported
only packages that the generic container base image
already provided; the restored library was never
actually needed. The defect surfaced only when a
repository imported a specialized modeling package absent
from the base image. The broader literature on why
deposited analyses fail to re-run [@trisovic2022]
documents how often re-execution simply fails. The
particular fault here is cross-boundary state, the state
that must pass from one step, shell, or process to the
next and silently does not. It is where CI bugs hide. A
dormant defect of this kind needs an adversarial input,
a dependency outside the comfortable base image, to bring
it to light. A check that passes tells us only that
nothing has yet exercised it hard enough to fail.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: capture versus validation

A colleague proposes to save CI minutes by deleting the
continuous-integration workflow from a compendium that
already has a committed `renv.lock` and `Dockerfile`.
They argue that since the lockfile and the container
'contain the reproducibility', removing CI cannot lower
the compendium's reproducibility level. Are they correct
about the level? Are they correct that nothing is lost?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

They are correct about the level and wrong about the
loss. The reproducibility level is set by what is
captured: the lockfile pins the packages (L1) and the
container pins the environment (L2). Continuous
integration captures nothing, so removing it leaves the
compendium at exactly the level it held before, L2. What
is lost is not level but assurance. Without CI, no one
tests, on a clean machine, that the captured environment
still rebuilds. The compendium becomes trusted rather
than tested. The silent decay of an external reference
(a package pulled from its repository, a base image
whose digest drifts) will go unnoticed until someone
tries a rebuild by hand.
:::
:::

## Secrets, tokens, and pinned actions {#sec-ci-secrets}

Before going further with verification, we pause on a
matter of hygiene. A CI runner holds credentials the
author's own laptop never needed, to comment on a pull
request, push a built image, or deploy a rendered report.
A leaked credential is a worse incident than a failed
reproducibility check. It warrants the same discipline
this chapter applies elsewhere: nothing should reach the
runner, or leave it, undeclared.

The first rule is never to let a secret reach a log or a
commit. GitHub's guidance on securing Actions workflows warns
that sensitive values 'should never be stored as plaintext in
workflow files' [@githubsecrets]. A workflow instead
references a stored secret through the `secrets` context,
`${{ secrets.NAME }}`. The runner substitutes the value at
execution time, and GitHub attempts to redact it from the
log. The redaction is best effort: 'automatic redaction is
not guaranteed', and the documentation recommends auditing
a workflow's output to confirm a secret is never
explicitly printed [@githubsecrets]. The condensed
workflow earlier in this chapter already follows the
pattern. Its line
`GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` passes a credential
into the job's environment without ever writing its value
into the file.

The second rule is least privilege. The default token GitHub
Actions issues a job is scoped broadly unless told otherwise,
and a workflow with no `permissions` block runs with more
access than most jobs need. GitHub's hardening guidance calls
a default of read-only repository contents 'good security
practice', with individual jobs granted more only where they
need it [@githubhardening]. The chapter's own example
already does this: it declares `permissions: contents: read`
at the top of the workflow.

The third rule has a direct parallel already established in
this book. @sec-containers showed that pinning a base image
by tag is not enough. A tag is a mutable pointer that a
maintainer can repoint to different bytes with no change to
the Dockerfile that names it; pinning by digest is what
actually fixes the bytes a build receives. A third-party
GitHub Action carries the same hazard. A
version tag such as `@v7` can be moved to a different commit
by its maintainer, or by anyone who compromises the
maintainer's account. The workflow that trusts the tag then
runs whatever that commit contains on its next trigger, with
no diff in the consuming repository to review. GitHub's own
hardening guidance recommends pinning a third-party action to
a full-length commit SHA rather than a tag. It states the
rationale plainly: a tag 'can be moved or deleted' by anyone
with write access to the action's repository, while forging a
given commit SHA would need an attacker to produce a SHA-1
collision [@githubhardening]:

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
```

The trailing comment records which release the SHA was
taken from, since forty hex characters say nothing to a
human reader. A SHA pin does not move on its own, so it
also does not pick up a security fix. Dependabot or
Renovate can watch the pinned actions and open a pull
request that replaces the SHA and its comment when a new
release appears, so that each update is a reviewed
commit rather than a silent change.

The chapter's own workflow examples fall short of their
own advice. They should be read as a teaching
simplification, not a model to copy unchanged. The
actions above (`actions/checkout@v7` and
`r-lib/actions/*@v2`) and the GitLab example's
`rocker/verse:4.6.1` all pin by tag. The CRAN gate tools
are installed at whatever version is current. Only
`zzrenvcheck`, which comes from a personal repository, is
pinned to a commit. This book's Dockerfile
explains a recipe by tag before showing the digest-pinned
version, and for the same reason: a tag is legible in a
worked example in a way forty hex characters are not.
A compendium's actual CI configuration should pin every
third-party action to a commit SHA, exactly as its
Dockerfile pins its base image by digest. A dependency
that can change with no commit to the project's own
history is undeclared state, whether it lives in a
package repository, a container registry, or an action's git
history.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what a version tag on an action actually promises

A teammate argues that pinning an action with `uses:
some-org/some-action@v3` is already safe, since the tag is
version-controlled and anyone can see which commit `v3` points
to on GitHub. What is wrong with this argument?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Visible is not the same as fixed. A tag is a label the
action's maintainer, or anyone with write access to that
repository, can repoint to a different commit at any time.
The workflow records only the label it asked for, not which
commit it ran last time. Checking what `v3` resolves to now
answers only 'what would run if I checked right now'. It
does not answer what ran last week, or what will run if the
tag moves before the next trigger. A commit SHA fixes the
content; a tag, however carefully maintained, is a pointer
that can be moved. This is exactly the distinction this
book already draws between a Docker tag and a Docker
digest.
:::
:::

## Two dialects: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI

We turn now from what the checks are to where they run.
Continuous integration is a general idea with several
implementations, and a health researcher should know at
least two, because the choice is often not theirs to make.
GitHub Actions and GitLab CI are two dialects of the same
underlying activity, and the difference between them is
one of syntax and hosting, not of principle.

The forge, the platform hosting the repository, matters
for research in a way it does not for general software
development. Research compendia are disproportionately
authored on institutional, often self-hosted, GitLab.
Many universities and laboratories run their own GitLab
servers and cannot, or will not, push a repository to
github.com. This is particularly so in Europe and
wherever data-governance rules discourage commercial
cloud hosting. Consider a clinical or registry study
whose data-handling agreement forbids external hosting.
For it, the ability to run the same reproducibility
checks on institutional GitLab is a precondition. A
framework that assumed GitHub would simply be unavailable
to a large part of its intended audience.

The two dialects differ structurally. GitHub Actions uses
one or more workflow files under `.github/workflows/`, each
organized into jobs and, within a job, a sequence of named
steps. GitLab CI uses a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` organized
into stages, each stage running a script. The same three
gates, expressed in the GitLab dialect, look like this.
We again show a static file that GitLab executes and this
book does not:

```yaml
stages:
  - gates
  - verify

gates:
  stage: gates
  # The tag must name the R version recorded in renv.lock.
  image: rocker/verse:4.6.1
  script:
    - Rscript -e 'renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)'
    - Rscript -e 'renv::install(c("rcmdcheck", "remotes",
        "pkgload"))'
    - Rscript -e 'remotes::install_github("rgt47/zzrenvcheck",
        ref = "6f53235668cb4048c1ae793d64b10d6505bf69a2")'
    # Gate 1: R CMD check of the package skin
    - Rscript -e 'rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck(args = "--no-manual",
        error_on = "warning")'
    # Gate 2: the dependency manifest, analysis/ included
    - Rscript -e 'zzrenvcheck::check_packages(strict = TRUE,
        error_on_fail = TRUE)'
    # Gate 3: the report re-renders from source
    - Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render(
        "analysis/report/report.Rmd",
        output_format = "html_document",
        output_dir = tempdir())'

verify:
  stage: verify
  # A shell-executor runner with Docker installed; the
  # tag is whatever the institution assigns to it.
  tags: [docker-shell]
  script:
    - docker build -t compendium:ci .
    - docker run --rm -e RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE
        -v "$PWD":/work -w /work
        compendium:ci Rscript ci/run-tests.R
```

The two files say the same thing in different words. Each
runs on the R version the lockfile records, restores the
pinned library into the project library, and installs the
gate tools beside it. Each then runs the three gates from
the repository root, so that every R step, and the check
subprocess it launches, sees the restored library; the
`.Rprofile` assumption of 'Where CI bugs hide' applies
to both. The image tag above names R 4.6.1, and this
book's own lockfile records R
4.6.1;
a compendium on another release names its own. The
`rocker/verse` image is used on GitLab because it ships
pandoc, which the render gate needs; on GitHub the
`setup-pandoc` action supplies it. Each script line is a
separate shell command, and GitLab fails the job at the
first one that exits with a nonzero status. Every gate
here can therefore fail the pipeline.

The second job, `verify`, rebuilds the project image and
runs the baseline tests inside it; it is the subject of
the next section. On GitLab it needs a runner that can
build images, which is an institutional decision. The
common alternative, Docker-in-Docker, requires a
privileged runner that many institutions do not allow.

On the plus side, maintaining a repository on
whichever forge an institution mandates is then a matter of
translating the dialect, and the checks carry over.
On the minus side, a workflow written twice, once per
dialect, is a workflow maintained twice. Every future
change must be made in two incompatible formats, a
standing divergence hazard. The resolution a mature
framework adopts is to single-source the logic in a
neutral place, the project's own `Makefile`. It holds one
target per gate (say `check`, `deps`, and `render`), each
carrying the commands shown above. Each forge's CI file
then shrinks to a thin shim that checks out the code and
calls `make`. The dialect differs only in its outermost
ten lines, and the checking behavior is defined once.

A further design point is that a workflow need not be
configured by hand: it can adapt itself to what the
repository contains. A feature is treated as present
exactly when its defining file exists. If `renv.lock` is
present, the workflow restores the pinned library;
otherwise it installs from `DESCRIPTION`. If a `Dockerfile`
or a Nix `flake.nix` is present, the workflow builds and
runs inside that environment; otherwise it runs on the
host runner. Such a workflow survives a project's toggling
of `renv` or of its container backend with no edit, and
one file can serve every archetype and every capture
level. The workflows in this chapter are not written that
way. They assume a compendium with both a lockfile and a
`Dockerfile`, so that every step is visible. A
presence-driven workflow wraps each step in a condition,
in GitHub's dialect `if: hashFiles('Dockerfile') != ''`.
That convenience has a cost to weigh. A
condition is also a way for a gate to disappear without
notice, since a misnamed file switches the step off and
the run stays green. A workflow that adapts should
therefore print which gates it ran and which it skipped.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the presence-driven trap

A presence-driven workflow skips the render gate when
`if: hashFiles('report.Rmd') != ''` evaluates to false.
Describe a concrete way this condition can silently
disable the gate without anyone intending it to, and what
single habit of the workflow catches the problem.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A rename, for instance moving `report.Rmd` to
`analysis-report.Rmd` during a reorganization, or a typo
in the condition itself, makes `hashFiles()` return an
empty string. The condition then evaluates to false and
the step is skipped. The job still reports success,
because a skipped step is not a failed one. Nothing in
the build output distinguishes 'rendered successfully'
from 'did not try to render'. The habit that catches it
is having the workflow print, for every conditional step,
whether it ran or was skipped. A silent skip is then
visible in the log, even though it does not turn the
build red.
:::
:::

## Verification and level L3

The first three gates confirm that the compendium builds,
checks, and renders on a clean machine. They do not
confirm that it produces the *same numbers*. That is the
work of verification, the L2-to-L3 transition and the top
of the ladder, which confirms what has been captured.

L3, as @sec-levels defines it, requires that recorded
outputs be shown to regenerate within a stated tolerance
from a clean rebuild. Each part of that sentence names a
mechanism. The recorded outputs and the tolerance live in
a *baseline test* (@sec-testing): a committed
file of key estimates is recorded once, and a test file
named `test-baseline-*.R` recomputes them and compares
with `expect_equal(..., tolerance = ...)`. The clean
rebuild is the project's own image, built from its
`Dockerfile` on a machine that has never seen it.
Verification is running the first inside the second, and
it fails if either fails. It fails if the image does not
rebuild, if any test fails, or if no baseline test runs
at all. A test suite without a baseline test can pass in
a rebuilt image and show that the environment is sound,
which is L2 confirmed. However, it has compared nothing
with a recorded result, so it is not L3.

In continuous integration this is a second job in the same
workflow, run after the gates pass:

```yaml
  verify:
    needs: gates
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # L2: the project's own Dockerfile must rebuild.
      - name: Rebuild the project image
        run: docker build -t compendium:ci .

      # L3: the test suite, with at least one baseline
      # test, must pass inside the rebuilt image.
      - name: Run the tests in the image
        run: >
          docker run --rm
          -e RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE
          -v "$PWD":/work -w /work
          compendium:ci Rscript ci/run-tests.R
```

The test step runs a short script from the repository.
The obvious one-line call,
`tinytest::run_test_dir('inst/tinytest')`, returns its
results and exits with status 0 even when an expectation
fails; we confirmed this with a deliberately failing test.
The script turns failures into a nonzero exit. It also
refuses to pass if no baseline test produced a result,
which is the case when the baseline file is missing or
when its guard found no data and exited early:

```r
# ci/run-tests.R
pkgload::load_all('.', quiet = TRUE)
res <- tinytest::run_test_dir('inst/tinytest')
print(res)
ran <- unique(as.data.frame(res)$file)
if (!any(grepl('^test-baseline', ran))) {
  stop('No baseline test ran, so this is not an L3 check.')
}
if (!tinytest::all_pass(res)) quit(status = 1)
```

Two assumptions are built in and should be checked
against the image in use. The image must contain
`tinytest` and `pkgload`, which means they must be in the
lockfile it restores. And because
`RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE` stops the mounted
project from activating its own library, the image must
already have the pinned packages on R's default path,
for example in the site library. The house rule applies here as
well. Changing one value in the committed baseline file
by more than the tolerance turns the job red at the
baseline expectation. Deleting or renaming the
`test-baseline-*.R` file turns it red at the 'no baseline
test ran' check. Breaking a `RUN` line in the
`Dockerfile` turns it red at the build. Against the toy
compendium, outside a container, we ran the first two. We
also ran a baseline file whose guard found no data and
exited early. Each run of the script exited with status
1, and the unbroken run exited with 0. The image build
and the job as a whole were not run for this chapter.

In the framework this book uses, the same composition is
the command `zzc verify`, which runs in two tiers. A
default *coherence* tier requires no rebuild. It checks
that the captured artifacts agree with each other and
that the R version named in the lockfile matches the one
in the Dockerfile. It also checks that the backend is
unambiguous, and that the raw data still matches its
recorded checksums. A `--full` *reproduction* tier
rebuilds the image and runs the test suite inside it. It
stamps L3 into the project's state record only when three
things hold: the image rebuilt, the tests passed, and at
least one `inst/tinytest/test-baseline*.R`
file exists and ran. Without a baseline test it reports
the project as rebuilt and tested, at L2, with no baseline
comparison, and does not stamp L3. Any later change to the
environment drops the stamp. A compendium that has
drifted therefore reverts to unverified automatically and
carries no stale claim. In regulated work, the stamp is not
a validation record: it carries no signer, no stated meaning
of a signature, and no quality review, which a controlled
record of validation status requires.

But what, precisely, should be compared? Verification
compares **computational outputs**, such as the row count
of a derived dataset, a fitted coefficient, or a
bootstrap bound, and *not* the rendered PDF or HTML. The
reason is that a rendered document is not a
deterministic function of the analysis. As @sec-literate
discussed, a PDF embeds the time of its creation and the
identifiers of the fonts the rendering machine happened to
have. Two renders of an unchanged analysis, minutes apart,
produce PDFs whose bytes differ, even though every number
in them is identical. Comparing PDFs would therefore
report a difference on every render and catch nothing real.
Comparing the estimates themselves, within a tolerance,
reports a difference exactly when a number changed by more
than floating-point noise, which is what we want to
detect. A hash is the right instrument for a file whose
bytes should not change, such as a raw data extract (the
next section). It is the wrong one for an estimate, whose
last binary digit can move under a different BLAS without
the analysis changing. There exist techniques to normalize
a document's embedded timestamps, by setting a fixed
`SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, and to freeze its fonts. With enough
care a byte-identical PDF is attainable. But the more
general practice is to verify the computational outputs
directly and leave the document to the render gate.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

The three gates do not reach L3; only the verify job
can, by running a baseline test in a rebuilt image. This
chapter ran the gate logic and the test script, but not
the image build or the job as a whole. A `verified` stamp
older than the last change to the lockfile, the
Dockerfile, or the code is stale, not an L3 claim. The
gates alone say nothing about whether the raw data
changed; the checksum manifest of the next section does.
In regulated work, an L3 stamp is also not a validation
record (@sec-testing). Nor is a hosted run a lasting
record: GitHub deletes workflow logs and artifacts after
90 days by default, a period an organization can
change within limits
[@githubretention]. A log or artifact that supports a
claim must therefore be downloaded and kept with the
records it supports, for as long as they are kept.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: trusting a stamp

A compendium was stamped `verified` three months ago. Last
week its `renv.lock` was updated to pin a new package
version, and CI has not run since. Is the `verified` stamp
still an honest L3 claim? Why or why not?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The stamp certifies that a specific, now-superseded
environment reproduced the baseline, not that the
environment as it currently stands does. Because the
lockfile changed after the last successful verification
run, the claim is stale: the thing the stamp describes no
longer exists. The honest statement is that the compendium
was L3 as of the old lockfile and is unverified now. This
is why a change to the environment should drop the stamp
automatically.
:::
:::

## Data integrity: the checksum manifest

We now turn to an input that sits outside everything the
lockfile and the container pin: the raw data itself. A
container fixes the software that reads the data, and a
lockfile fixes the packages. However, neither notices if
the data file on disk is silently altered between the
analysis and its re-execution (a row edited, a value
corrected, a column recoded). An altered input produces a
changed result with no error and no warning.

The guard is a **checksum manifest**, a small file,
conventionally `data-manifest.sha256`, that records the
SHA-256 checksum of each raw data file. Verification reads
the manifest, recomputes the checksum of each file as it
now stands, and reports a mismatch. Because any change to
a file's bytes changes its checksum, a silently altered
input is caught the next time verification runs.

To illustrate, consider a small synthetic example. We
write a tiny data file to disk, record its checksum,
write the same values again from a different kind of R
object, write a third copy with a single value altered,
and hash each file. The checksum is computed from the
file's bytes, not from the R object in memory. The point
to observe is that a one-cell change, a shift of a
single outcome from 11.1 to 11.2, produces a completely
different digest, so the alteration cannot pass
unnoticed.


::: {#tbl-integrity .cell tbl-cap='A single altered value changes the digest of a data file. The three CSV files are hashed by their bytes on disk. The second holds the same values as the first, written from a plain data frame rather than a tibble, and its digest matches. The third differs in exactly one cell, and its SHA-256 digest differs from the first character, so a checksum manifest detects the change.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tibble)
library(digest)
library(knitr)

cohort <- tibble(
  id      = 1:5,
  arm     = c('treatment', 'placebo', 'treatment',
              'placebo', 'treatment'),
  outcome = c(12.4, 9.8, 11.1, 10.3, 13.0)
)

hash_csv <- function(x) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = '.csv')
  write.csv(x, path, row.names = FALSE)
  digest(file = path, algo = 'sha256')
}

altered <- cohort
altered$outcome[3] <- 11.2

digests <- c(hash_csv(cohort),
             hash_csv(as.data.frame(cohort)),
             hash_csv(altered))

manifest <- tibble(
  file = c('cohort.csv (baseline)',
           'same values, from a data.frame',
           'one cell altered'),
  digest_first16 = substr(digests, 1, 16),
  matches_baseline = ifelse(digests == digests[1],
                            'yes', 'no')
)

kable(
  manifest,
  col.names = c('File', 'SHA-256 (first 16 chars)',
                'Matches baseline'),
  align = 'llc'
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|File                           |SHA-256 (first 16 chars) | Matches baseline |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------|:----------------:|
|cohort.csv (baseline)          |cc03e329ae1b1114         |       yes        |
|same values, from a data.frame |cc03e329ae1b1114         |       yes        |
|one cell altered               |632857fa64a59ad4         |        no        |


:::
:::


The altered file's digest differs from the first
character, although the files differ in a single cell.
That sensitivity to any change is what makes a checksum a
reliable integrity guard. Suppose a verification run
recomputes these digests and finds the third where it
expected the first. It has then caught an altered input,
and has done so without needing to know what the correct
value was, only that it has changed since the manifest
was recorded. The second row shows why the file, and not
the object, is what gets hashed. Hashing the tibble and
the data frame themselves with `digest()` would serialize
each object, class attributes included, and give two
different digests for identical values: here
`digest(cohort) == digest(as.data.frame(cohort))` is
FALSE.
The bytes on disk carry only the values.

A manifest line pairs a digest with a path, in the format
`shasum -a 256` writes and `shasum -a 256 -c` checks. For
this book's raw extract it reads:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
raw_path <- '../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'
cat(digest(file = raw_path, algo = 'sha256'), '  ',
    'analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv', '\n', sep = '')
#> aec0973593e41aa0186ca57d44949a369323a71d9e21fcc25d6cc025b134aea7  analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv
```
:::
