## Proving the framework itself: the capture test matrix

One rung below the compendium's own verification sits an
easily overlooked question: how does the framework know that a
project configured for, say, L1
actually reaches L1? A claim that a given combination of
toggles produces a given level is itself a claim that can
be tested, and a responsible framework tests it rather
than asserting it.

The instrument is a **capture test matrix**. It scaffolds
a throwaway compendium for each combination of the capture
axes: the package backend present or absent, and the
container environment present or absent. For each, it
asserts that the result passes `R CMD check`, is a
loadable workspace, and sits at its stated level. The
matrix has the following shape. Its axes are the capture
axes; CI is the harness that runs the matrix, not a
dimension of it.

| Backend (`renv`) | Environment (Docker) | Level | Assertion |
|---|---|---|---|
| off | off | L0 | check passes; valid workspace |
| on  | off | L1 | check passes; `renv` activates on host |
| off | on  | L0 | check passes; image installs from `DESCRIPTION`, so the environment is fixed but the packages are unpinned |
| on  | on  | L2 | check passes; image restores from lockfile |

The third row sits at L0 although it builds an image,
because the rungs are cumulative. L2 presupposes the
lockfile of L1, and an image that installs from
`DESCRIPTION` pins no package version.

Two points about the matrix deserve emphasis. First, Nix,
the alternative backend of @sec-backends, is verified as a
*substitution*. It replaces the `renv`-plus-Docker
combination and must reach L2 on its own, so it is
checked as a peer of that combination rather than added
as a fourth column. Second, the configuration that
renders a report with `renv` on but Docker off is, in
practice, the most error-prone, and it is exercised
explicitly. Because container builds under emulation are
expensive, the matrix is tiered. The host-only rows run
on every pull request, and the rows that build an image
run on merge and on a nightly schedule.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: testing the claim, not just the tool

Why does a responsible framework test the claim 'this
combination of toggles reaches level L1' rather than
simply asserting it in documentation?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because the claim is itself a factual statement about
behavior, not a design intention. Design intentions
drift from implementation the same way an undeclared
dependency drifts from a lockfile. That is, a later
change to the scaffolding code can silently break the L1
configuration while the documentation still describes the
old behavior. Asserting the claim in prose is exactly the
kind of trust-without-test this whole chapter argues
against. The capture test matrix applies the chapter's
own standard to the framework that makes the claim.
:::
:::

## How continuous integration adapts to the archetype

Continuous integration adapts its gates to the archetype;
@tbl-archetype-weight in @sec-compendium is the reference.
Of the three gates of this chapter, `R CMD check` and the
dependency-manifest gate are universal, run by every
archetype. The latter, however, runs in an
archetype-conditional form. It is the strict
`DESCRIPTION`-inclusion check for an R package, and the
weaker
$\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{renv.lock}$ inclusion for
a compendium, as the section on the three gates
established. The
render gate is the conditional one. It is present
wherever a report exists, and absent from an
**R-package archetype**, which has none.

The case most worth stating here is the
**simulation archetype**, which raises a distinct concern
of cost. A full run can take hours or days. The idiomatic
arrangement therefore runs a *reduced* pipeline under CI:
a handful of iterations with a fixed seed, enough to
confirm the pipeline executes and the outputs have the
right shape. The full pipeline runs elsewhere, on a
cluster or a scheduled job, and is verified against a
baseline separately. The seeding discipline of
@sec-testing is what makes the reduced run meaningful. A
fixed seed makes even a short run reproducible, so CI
checks reproducibility rather than merely execution. The
presence-driven workflow discovers the archetype from
what the repository contains. The analyst's contribution
is therefore to ensure the archetype and its gates are
matched.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: when a package does need the render gate

An R-package archetype is said to have no report, so no
render gate. Under what condition does the render gate
apply to a package archetype after all, and what does it
render in that case?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The render gate applies whenever the package ships a
vignette, which is itself a rendered document. The gate
re-renders `vignettes/intro.Rmd` (or whichever vignette
files exist) on every push. It confirms that the
vignette's code still runs against the restored library,
exactly the check a manuscript's report receives. Only a
package with
neither a report nor a vignette has nothing for
the render gate to do.
:::
:::

## Independent external verification

The checking we have described so far is the author's own,
run on the author's forge against the author's baseline. It
is necessary and it is not sufficient. An author who has
misunderstood their own reproducibility can build a CI
pipeline that faithfully confirms the misunderstanding.
The complement is verification from outside the project
entirely, by someone with no stake in its passing.

The most developed such scheme is CODECHECK, described by
Nust and Eglen [@nust2021codecheck]. In it an independent
codechecker re-executes an analysis during peer review,
on their own machine, and issues a certificate recording
what was run and what was reproduced. The value of the
exercise lies exactly in its independence. The
codechecker carries none of the author's undeclared
state; this is the same property that makes a CI runner
effective, here held by a person instead of a virtual
machine. In a parallel development, major computing
venues have formalized artifact review and badging. Under
it, a submission's computational artifacts are evaluated
and, if they reproduce, marked with a badge on the
published paper [@acm2020]. Stodden and colleagues have
documented the persistence of the reproducibility
problem. They have also documented the effectiveness,
and limits, of journal policies that attempt to compel
deposition and checking [@stodden2018]. The ten-rules
literature, for its part, places independent re-execution
among its recommendations [@sandve2013].

These schemes validate and capture nothing: they add no
lockfile and no container, only a second, independent
execution of the analysis. Continuous integration is a
machine that is not yours, and independent verification
is a person who is not you. Both
catch the reproducibility failures that the author's own
generous machine had hidden, at the last responsible
moment before a result enters the scientific record.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what independence adds beyond CI

An author's CI pipeline passes every gate, including
verification against a baseline. Why might a CODECHECK
reviewer still find something CI did not, given that both
are described as 'a machine, or a person, that is not
yours'?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

CI is configured by the author, so it tests what the
author thought to test, against a baseline the author
recorded, in an environment the author specified. If the
author misunderstood what the analysis was supposed to
produce, or recorded a baseline after a bug had already
entered it, CI will faithfully and indefinitely confirm
the misunderstanding. A codechecker reads the paper and
forms an independent judgment of what the analysis should
produce. The codechecker then checks the artifacts against
that judgment rather than against the author's own
configuration, which is a check CI structurally cannot
perform on itself.
:::
:::

## Worked example

To make the machinery concrete, consider a plausible
sequence of events in a cohort-study compendium, of the
kind that recurs in practice.

The analyst is refining a model and, mid-session, reaches
for a package that computes robust standard errors,
`sandwich`. They install it interactively with
`install.packages()`, and add `library(sandwich)` to
`analysis/scripts/02_model.R`, which the report sources.
They obtain the result they wanted, and commit. On their
own machine everything runs: the package is installed,
the script loads it, the report renders, the numbers
appear. The compendium looks, to its author, finished.

The push triggers CI, and the fresh runner tells a
different story, though not at the gate a reader might
expect. The runner checks out the committed files and
restores the pinned library from `renv.lock`. This
lockfile was never updated, because the interactive
install was never snapshotted. Gate 1, `R CMD check`,
passes. It is not at fault: the script lives in
`analysis/`, which the build excludes, so the check never
reads it. Gate 2, the dependency-manifest gate, reads
`analysis/` and goes red. It names `sandwich` as a
package the code uses and the lockfile does not pin. Had
that gate been absent, gate 3 would have failed the same
run from the other direction. The report sources the
script, the script calls `library(sandwich)`, and the
restored library has no such package, so the render stops
at that chunk. Either way, CI has found on a clean
machine precisely the undeclared state the author's
machine supplied silently. Had the workflow run only
`R CMD check`, as many compendium workflows do, the build
would have been green.

The fix is not to weaken the check but to repair the
capture. The analyst records the new package in the
lockfile by snapshotting the environment, commits the
updated `renv.lock`, and pushes again. This time the
runner restores a library that contains the package. The
dependency gate passes, the report renders, and the gates
go green. The `verify` job then rebuilds the image from
the new lockfile and runs the baseline test. This is
where the analyst learns whether the change moved a
recorded result, such as a confidence limit. If it did,
the baseline is re-recorded deliberately, in a commit
that says why, not loosened until it passes.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: which gate, and why

In the worked example, `R CMD check` passes even though
`sandwich` is in fact unpinned. Why does this gate miss
the defect that the dependency-manifest gate catches,
and is that a flaw in `R CMD check`?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

It is not a flaw; it is a scope limit stated earlier in
the chapter. `R CMD check` runs on the package `R CMD
build` produces, and `.Rbuildignore` excludes
`analysis/`, so the check never parses, runs, or scans the
script that calls `library(sandwich)`. The gate is doing
what it is specified to do, checking the package skin.
The defect lives one directory outside that skin, which
is why a compendium needs a second gate that does read
`analysis/`.
:::
:::

## Debugging a failed reproduction

The worked example above is the easy case: CI catches the
defect the same day, on the same commit that introduced it.
The harder case arrives later. A compendium that rendered
cleanly in March fails in October, when a reviewer clones
it, a collaborator resumes it, or the author themselves
reruns it for a revision. Nothing in this section is
generic R debugging, which is out of scope for this book.
It is a diagnostic sequence specific to one question: it
worked before, and it does not now, so what changed?

The first move is to localize the failure in time, not in
code. Suppose the history between the last known-good
state and the present failure holds more than a handful
of commits. Reading each one is then slower than letting
git find the boundary. `git bisect` does this by binary
search. Told one commit that is good and one that is bad,
it checks out the midpoint and asks for a verdict,
halving the remaining range at each step.

```bash
git bisect start <bad-commit> <good-commit>
git bisect run Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd")'
git bisect reset
```

`git bisect run` automates the verdict. It checks out each
candidate commit and runs the given command, taking a
nonzero exit status as 'bad' and zero as 'good'. It
continues until a single first-bad commit remains. We
verified the mechanism on a disposable four-commit toy
repository, under git 2.55.0. The first commit
established a check that passed. The second, an
unrelated-looking refactor, silently changed a value the
check depended on, and two further commits added only
comments. We marked the fourth commit bad and the first
good with `git bisect start`, then ran
`git bisect run Rscript check.R`. It
tested the midpoint, found it still bad, and tested the
commit below that. It then named the second commit as the
first bad one, in two bisection steps rather than three
linear checks. The command handed to `bisect run` need
not be a toy. It can be the render gate or a baseline
test from @sec-testing, which is exactly what lets the
search run unattended across dozens of commits.

Once the boundary commit is known, the next question is
whether the commit changed code, or whether something
outside the commit changed under it, because `git bisect`
can only blame a commit if the environment at each
checkout is otherwise identical. Consider a pipeline that
reruns the same pinned commit weeks apart and gets a
different answer. It did not fail because of anything in
the diff, and the fix is to compare environments, not
history. `sessionInfo()` (@sec-dependencies
and the glossary) is the cheapest comparison. It is run
in the working environment and the failing one, and the
two are diffed by eye for an R version, platform, or
package version that moved. `renv::status()` goes
further, comparing the project library with the
lockfile and reporting packages that are missing or
installed at a different version. It is the first thing
to run when the suspicion is drift in the restored
library rather than in the
analysis code. When the suspicion lands on the
lockfile itself, `git diff <good-sha> <bad-sha> -- renv.lock`
shows exactly which package or version entries changed
between the two commits. This narrows 'something in the
environment changed' to the one or two packages
responsible.

If the analysis is a `targets` pipeline (@sec-pipelines),
the diagnostic moves from history into the dependency
graph. `tar_outdated()` lists which targets the pipeline
considers stale and therefore due to rerun.
`tar_visnetwork()` draws the same information as a graph.
The analyst can then see where in the chain of targets
the invalidation begins, rather than at which commit it
was introduced. This is the pipeline-native counterpart
to bisecting, since `targets` already tracks what depends
on what. The question 'what broke, and what does it
affect' can therefore be answered from the dependency
graph instead of from commit history. This holds provided
the pipeline's metadata store, `_targets/`, survived the
problem. On a fresh CI runner it is absent unless it was
committed or the workflow restores it, and a pipeline
run there without it rebuilds every target.

The last diagnostic is reading a CI log on its own terms.
This chapter has already named the three gates and the
discipline of reproducing a failure exactly as CI ran it,
not as is convenient to invoke by hand ('Where CI bugs
hide', above). Applied to a failed reproduction, that
discipline has three parts. First, identify which of the
three gates reported red: `R CMD check`, the dependency
manifest, or the render. Second, read what it printed,
not just that it failed, since the WARNING text or the
`stop()` message names the missing package or the broken
chunk directly. Third, reproduce that exact step locally,
from a session with the same restored library CI used.
This is preferable to re-running the whole render and
hoping the same failure reappears in a more informative
form.

None of these five moves is a substitute for the others, and
the order matters more than any single step. Bisection is
cheap to run and narrows the search space before anything
else is attempted. Session-info and lockfile comparisons
cost nothing once the boundary commit is known. They
settle, quickly, whether the defect is in the diff or in
the environment around it. `targets` diagnostics apply
only when a pipeline is involved. Reading the CI log
carefully is usually the last step, because by the time
it is needed the first four moves have already said which
gate to expect it from.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: bisecting an environment problem

A pipeline's render step fails on a Tuesday rerun of a commit
that rendered cleanly the previous Friday. The commit has not
changed. Why will `git bisect` be useless here, and what
should be compared instead?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

`git bisect` localizes a failure to a commit by checking out
different revisions and testing each one, which only works
when the thing that changed is in the history it walks. Here
the commit is fixed and identical on both days, so bisection
has nothing to vary and nothing to find; every checkout it
tries is the same code. The defect lies outside the commit,
most likely in the restored environment: an unpinned
dependency that resolved to a different version between
Friday and Tuesday, or a base image whose tag moved. The
right comparison is `sessionInfo()` or
`renv::status()` run on both days. If the lockfile
itself is suspect, it is a diff of `renv.lock` against the
copy captured on Friday. It is not a bisection across
commits that never changed.
:::
:::

## Demonstrating a gate on the cohort compendium

The logic that runs on a CI runner also runs, in
miniature, on this book's own cohort compendium, without
any CI infrastructure at all. Below, a short script
mirrors the dependency-manifest gate of the earlier
section. It finds every package `R/cohort.R` actually
uses, compares that list against what this compendium
currently declares as pinned, and reports whether the
gate passes.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
used <- unique(renv::dependencies('../../R/cohort.R')$Package)
#> Finding R package dependencies ... Done!
locked <- names(renv::lockfile_read('../../renv.lock')$Packages)
base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = 'base'))

gate_check <- function(missing) {
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop('Used but not pinned in renv.lock: ', toString(missing))
  }
  'gate passed'
}

missing_now <- setdiff(used, c(locked, base_pkgs))
cat('Packages R/cohort.R uses:', toString(used), '\n')
#> Packages R/cohort.R uses: parallel, stats, survival, tibble, utils, withr
cat('Missing from the pinned set:',
    if (length(missing_now)) toString(missing_now) else '(none)', '\n')
#> Missing from the pinned set: (none)
cat('Result:', gate_check(missing_now), '\n')
#> Result: gate passed
```
:::




The gate passes. `R/cohort.R` uses
`parallel`, `stats`, `survival`, `tibble`, `utils`, and `withr`, and each is either pinned in `renv.lock` or part of base R.
The house rule of this book applies
here as well: a gate shown only to pass has not been
shown to work. We therefore run the same script against a
`used` list with the chapter's own running example of an
unpinned dependency added. It shows what a real CI log
would print the moment someone adds `library(sandwich)`
to a cohort script without snapshotting it:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
used_broken <- c(used, 'sandwich')
missing_broken <- setdiff(used_broken, c(locked, base_pkgs))
result <- tryCatch(gate_check(missing_broken),
                   error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat('Missing from the pinned set:', toString(missing_broken), '\n')
#> Missing from the pinned set: sandwich
cat('Result:', result, '\n')
#> Result: Used but not pinned in renv.lock: sandwich
```
:::


The injected package is named, and the step would stop
with a nonzero exit status in real CI. The failure points
at the undeclared dependency, which is what the
dependency-manifest gate is for. Restoring `used` to its
real value (dropping the injected `sandwich`) returns the
gate to green, as reverting the offending commit would on
a real runner.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what this demonstration does and does not show

This section ran the dependency-gate logic locally, inside
the rendered report, rather than on an actual CI runner.
What does that leave unverified about the compendium's
real CI setup, if one exists?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Running the logic locally confirms the gate's *logic* is
correct: it finds the right packages and reports the
right ones as missing. However, it says nothing about
whether a real workflow file invokes that logic
correctly, or restores the right library before running
it. Nor does it show that the job actually stops on
failure rather than printing a warning and continuing.
Those are the cross-boundary and
`error_on` pitfalls the chapter described earlier, and only
an actual CI run, on an actual fresh runner, can confirm
them.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A large language model is a capable assistant for CI work,
which is heavy on boilerplate YAML. It is also a
hazardous one, because CI failures are subtle and a
plausible-looking workflow can still be wrong. We give
three prompt patterns, each with what to watch for and
what the analyst must independently verify.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

One rule comes first (habit 3). Never paste or upload
protected health information, identifiable records, or data
held under a data use agreement, nor outputs derived from
them, into a model or a coding agent unless three conditions
all hold. The institution has approved that endpoint for
that class of data. The IRB protocol and the consent permit
the processing. The data use agreement, or the provider's
terms, permits it. If any of the three is unclear, the
answer is no.

The third condition is the one most often missed.
Institutional approval of a tool does not override the terms
under which a data provider released the data. NIH, for
example, treats sharing controlled-access data with
third-party generative AI tools through prompts as a breach
of the data use certification, and a model trained on such
data as a derivative that may not be distributed without
approval [@nihgenai2025].

Describe the structure instead: the column names and types,
or a small synthetic example generated from the data
dictionary, never edited from real rows. A coding agent sees
whatever files are in its working tree, so run it in a
checkout or container where the real data is not mounted.

An agent also acts: it runs commands, edits files, and can
commit and push. Let it work on a branch and propose changes
by pull request. Review every change to tests, baselines, the
lockfile, and CI configuration line by line, and keep merges,
pushes, deposits, and history rewrites for yourself
(@sec-llm-delegate).
:::


CI touches data in ways that are easy to miss. A CI log
that prints rows of a failing render or test is a derived
output in the sense of the rule above, so a log excerpt is
pasted only after those rows are removed. For CI work the
structure to describe is the workflow file and the error
message.

**Prompt.** 'Write a GitHub Actions workflow that runs `R
CMD check` on my compendium inside the `rocker/tidyverse`
container and restores packages from `renv.lock`.'

*Watch for.* A workflow that restores the library in one
step and runs the check in another without ensuring the
restored library reaches the check subprocess. As we saw,
adjusting the library path in one step does not carry to
the next, and `R CMD check` runs in a child process that
sees only the library path it is handed. Check for the
naive two-step form, which passes only when every
dependency happens to be in the base image. Watch also
for `error_on = 'error'`, a dependency
step that reports without failing, and
`continue-on-error: true`. Each of these leaves a gate
that cannot go red. Remember, too, that `R CMD check`
alone never looks at `analysis/`.

*Verification.* Do not trust the workflow because it is
syntactically valid. Confirm it fails correctly by
introducing a deliberate gap: import a specialized
package absent from the base image, do not restore it,
and check that the build goes red. A CI check that has
never been seen to fail has not been shown to work.
Seeing means reading the run log yourself: a coding
agent's report that 'CI is green' is a claim about the
run, not an observation of it.

An agent asked to make a failing build pass can reach
green by the patterns this triple lists, adding
`continue-on-error: true` or loosening `error_on`, and
the change arrives as an ordinary commit. Treat
`.github/workflows/` as a protected path and read every
line of any diff that touches it before it merges. CI is
also where embedded instructions matter most. An agent
that reads a log, an issue, or a downloaded file can be
steered by text planted in it, and in CI it may run with
the repository's secrets. Grant its jobs the least
privilege of @sec-ci-secrets, and keep pushes and
merges with the analyst (@sec-llm-delegate).

**Prompt.** 'Add a verification step that checks my analysis
reproduces, by hashing the output and comparing it to a
saved value.'

*Watch for.* A step that hashes the rendered PDF or HTML.
The report is the most visible output and the wrong
thing to hash, because its bytes carry timestamps and
font identifiers and change on every render.

*Verification.* Insist that the target is a computational
output. Estimates should be compared with a committed
baseline within a stated tolerance, in a
`test-baseline-*.R` file, while hashes are kept for files
whose bytes should not change. Confirm by rendering the
report twice without changing the analysis: the report's
own bytes should differ while the baseline test still
passes. If the model's chosen target changes between the
two renders, it is the wrong target.

**Prompt.** 'My compendium is a simulation study that takes
six hours to run. Write CI for it.'

*Watch for.* A workflow that attempts the full run on every
push, which will time out or consume the CI budget, or one
that runs so few iterations that it no longer tests
anything meaningful.

*Verification.* Confirm the workflow runs a reduced,
fixed-seed pipeline under CI and defers the full run
elsewhere. Check that the reduced run is seeded so that
its short output is itself reproducible. Verify that the
number of iterations in the reduced run is large enough to
exercise the code paths that matter, not merely one.

*A better prompt.* 'My compendium's simulation runs
`<B>` replicates in about six hours; `R/` holds the
functions and `inst/tinytest/` the tests. Write a GitHub
Actions workflow that, on each push, runs the tests and
a fixed-seed run of `<b>` replicates within 20 minutes,
pins each action by commit SHA, and never sets
`continue-on-error`. Say where the full run should
happen instead, and what deliberate change I should
make to confirm that each step can fail.'

In each case a syntactically valid workflow is the easy
part to check. The semantics, what the check actually
proves and whether it can fail for the right reason, are
what the analyst must verify and cannot delegate.

## Exercise 1

The ladder grades **capture**: how far down the determinant
stack a result is locked. CI locks nothing. It installs no
package into the lockfile and no library into the image, so
removing it leaves every pinned layer exactly as pinned as
before. A compendium at L2 with CI and the same compendium
at L2 without it sit on the same rung.

**What is lost is assurance rather than level.** Without CI
nobody rebuilds the captured environment on a clean machine
and re-runs the analysis in it. The compendium becomes
trusted rather than tested, and the distance between 'this
should rebuild' and 'this does rebuild' stops being
measured.

**A concrete failure.** A base image is repointed by its
maintainer and the Dockerfile pins it by tag rather than
digest, so the environment changes underneath the
project. With CI, the next push rebuilds and the check
fails, naming the day it broke. Without CI, the compendium
looks healthy on the author's machine, where an old image
is cached locally. It then fails for the first reader who
builds it from scratch, possibly years later, with no
indication of when or why it broke. Equally good answers
include a package pulled from CRAN and no longer
restorable, or a system library the analysis silently
depended on and never declared. A chunk that only ever
ran because of state left in the author's session is
another.

## Exercise 2

**`R CMD check`** catches a defect in the package skin as
code. One example is a function in `R/` calling a package
that is used but not declared in `DESCRIPTION` (a
WARNING, so the gate must fail on warnings). Others are a
syntax error in a file under `R/` that nothing currently
calls, or a documented argument that no longer exists.
The render gate would not see it if the report does not
touch that function. The manifest gate checks
declarations rather than whether the code loads.
The same defects under `analysis/` are invisible to
`R CMD check`, which never sees that directory.

**The render gate** catches a defect that appears only when
the document is built. Examples are a chunk that fails on
a clean machine because it read an uncommitted file, a
figure whose code errors, or a cross-reference to a label
that no longer exists. `R CMD check` never renders, so it
sees none of this.

**The dependency-manifest gate** catches drift between the
code and the manifests: a package used in a script under
`analysis/` and missing from `renv.lock`, which
`R CMD check` never sees, or, for the package archetype,
a package declared in `DESCRIPTION` and missing from
`renv.lock`. The code may load and the
document may render perfectly on a machine where the
package happens to be installed, so neither other gate
fires.

**A failure none of the three catches:** a change in the
*data*. A raw extract silently replaced with a corrected
version leaves the code valid, the document renderable,
and the manifests consistent. Meanwhile every number in
the report changes. All three gates pass. The
**data-integrity gate** addresses it, by hashing the
inputs and derived outputs and comparing against a
recorded manifest.

The **verification gate** addresses the adjacent case in
which the code changes a result without any of the three
noticing. It does so by comparing computed outputs
against recorded baselines.
:::

## Exercise 3


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(digest)
m1 <- lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort)
d1 <- digest(coef(m1), algo = 'sha256')

m2 <- lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort)
same_refit <- digest(coef(m2), algo = 'sha256') == d1
same_refit
#> [1] TRUE

cohort_alt <- cohort
cohort_alt$outcome[1] <- cohort_alt$outcome[1] + 1
m3 <- lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort_alt)
same_altered <- digest(coef(m3), algo = 'sha256') == d1
same_altered
#> [1] FALSE
```
:::


Refitting the identical model to identical data, in the
same session, gives an identical digest; altering one
outcome value changes it. The chunk above, run on R
4.6.0 when this book was rendered, returned
TRUE and then FALSE.

**Why the digest is sensitive to any change.** The
coefficients are a deterministic function of the data and
the model specification. Nothing about the time of
fitting, the machine's fonts, or the session's history
enters them, so within one session and platform the digest
changes exactly when a number changes and not otherwise.

**Why it is still the wrong tool for verification.** A
digest compares serialized *bytes*, not numeric *values*.
R's own documentation for `serialize()` (the mechanism
`digest()` and `saveRDS()` both rely on) states that the
default serialization format changed from version 2 to
version 3 in R 3.6.0. It also warns explicitly that 'the
serialization format may change in future versions of R, so
this interface should not be used for long-term storage of
R objects' (`?serialize`, inspected). Nothing guarantees
that two R versions, or two platforms, serialize an
identical numeric vector to identical bytes. An added
attribute, a changed internal representation, or a future
format bump can flip the digest while every coefficient is
still correct to the last bit. That makes a coefficient
digest a plausible false-positive generator across
upgrades. This is exactly the failure mode this book's
baseline test is built to avoid, by comparing *values*
with `expect_equal(..., tolerance = ...)` rather than
comparing serialized bytes with `==`. The digests in
@tbl-integrity are defensible because they hash the bytes
of a data file on disk, not a serialized R object, and
byte-for-byte identity of a raw data file is the actual
requirement. Reused on a fitted model's
coefficients, it answers a different, stricter question
('are the bytes identical') than the one a
reproducibility check needs answered ('is the value the
same within tolerance'). It will occasionally answer it
wrong in a way that looks like a false alarm.

One practical refinement the exercise invites. Digesting
the whole `lm` object rather than `coef()` is fragile,
because the object stores the call and a `terms`
environment, which can carry incidental references. Hashing
the coefficient vector, or a named list of the quantities
actually reported, is more robust against incidental
differences. However, it does not remove the
cross-version risk above. A baseline test with a stated
tolerance remains the right tool for verifying that an
estimate has not drifted.

**Why hashing a plot would not be sound.** A rendered plot
is an image file. Image files embed creation timestamps,
are affected by device version and font availability, and
can differ in their compression between runs. Two plots
of the identical model can differ byte for byte while
depicting exactly the same thing. The check would
therefore fail on every rebuild and carry no information.
The rule this generalizes to is that verification hashes
computational outputs, not rendered artifacts; it is the
same rule that governs the PDF in @sec-literate.
:::

## Exercise 4

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [gates]

gates:
  stage: gates
  image: rocker/verse:4.6.1
  script:
    - Rscript -e 'renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)'
    - Rscript -e 'renv::install(c("rcmdcheck", "remotes"))'
    - Rscript -e 'remotes::install_github("rgt47/zzrenvcheck",
        ref = "6f53235668cb4048c1ae793d64b10d6505bf69a2")'
    # Gate 1: fails on a WARNING, as error-on does on GitHub
    - Rscript -e 'rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck(args = "--no-manual",
        error_on = "warning")'
    # Gate 2: the target that modifies nothing
    - make check-renv-no-fix
    # Gate 3: render inside this image, without Docker
    - Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render(
        "analysis/report/report.Rmd",
        output_format = "html_document",
        output_dir = tempdir())'
```

**The two structural differences.**

*Jobs and steps versus stages and scripts.* GitHub Actions
composes a job from reusable `uses:` steps, each a
versioned action maintained elsewhere. The workflow
therefore reads as an assembly of components. GitLab CI
defines
stages containing jobs whose bodies are shell scripts, so
the pipeline reads as commands in an image. The GitHub
form is more declarative and depends on an ecosystem of
actions; the GitLab form is more direct and depends on
nothing but the image.

*Per-file versus single-file configuration.* GitHub reads
every file under `.github/workflows/`, so a project
naturally accumulates several workflows with separate
triggers. GitLab reads a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` at the
root, so everything is expressed in one file with rules
selecting what runs when.

**Why a Makefile shrinks both.** The differences above are
entirely about *orchestration*: what runs, in what order,
on what trigger. The check logic itself, run `R CMD check`,
render the report, verify the manifests, is identical in
both and belongs in neither file. Putting it behind named
targets leaves each CI file a thin shim naming the image
and calling a short list of them. The logic is then
single-sourced, testable locally with the same command CI
runs, and portable to a third forge for the cost of one
more shim.

A zzcollab-scaffolded compendium's `Makefile` already
ships targets for this, but not every target is a gate,
and the file above calls only one of them. Three cautions
apply. First, `check-renv` runs the dependency check with
`auto_fix = TRUE` and is meant to be run before a commit.
On a runner it repairs `renv.lock` in place, so it
reports success for the very omission the gate exists to
catch. Its sibling `check-renv-no-fix` modifies nothing
and exits nonzero on failure, and only that target is a
gate. Second, `check` runs `R CMD check --as-cran`, which
exits nonzero on an ERROR but not on a WARNING, so an
undeclared import passes it; the file therefore calls
`rcmdcheck` with `error_on = "warning"` directly. Third,
the render targets (`docker-render`, `docker-render-qmd`,
`docker-render-book`) start a container with
`docker run`. A job whose `image:` is `rocker/verse` has
no Docker daemon, so the file renders inside the image
itself, after the `renv::restore()` that the body's
GitLab file also performs. Rendering through the
project's own image belongs in a job on a runner that can
run Docker, as the `verify` job above does. If you adapt
this exercise to your own compendium, name the targets
that match it, and confirm that each one can fail.
:::

## Exercise 5

**Data analysis:** `R CMD check` and the manifest gate
always; the render gate if a report is produced.
**Manuscript:** all three, since the rendered document is
the deliverable. **R package:** `R CMD check` and the
manifest gate; the render gate only if a vignette exists.
**Simulation:** `R CMD check` and the manifest gate; the
render gate if a report is produced, plus a
seed-determinism check. **Blog:** the render gate above
all, since the deliverable is the site. `R CMD check`
and the manifest gate apply to any code the posts run.

**Arranging the simulation.** CI runs a reduced pipeline:
the same driver, the same functions, the same seed. The
replicate count is set by a parameter to something small,
perhaps a hundred replicates in place of a hundred
thousand. The full pipeline runs elsewhere, on a cluster,
and its outputs are recorded and deposited.

**What the fixed seed contributes.** It is what makes the
reduced run a genuine reproducibility test rather than a
smoke test. With the seed fixed, the first hundred
replicates of the reduced run are *the same hundred
replicates* the full run begins with. Their summary is
therefore a deterministic value that can be recorded and
compared exactly. Without the seed, the reduced run could
only be checked against a tolerance derived from Monte
Carlo error. That is a much weaker statement, and one
that passes even when the generator has changed.

The limit is that the reduced run verifies that the
machinery reproduces, not that the full study's estimates
are correct, since a hundred replicates estimate the
target quantity poorly.
:::

## Exercise 6

**The shared role.** Both are an independent re-execution
of the analysis in an environment the author does not
control, performed by a party who has no stake in it
succeeding. A CI runner does this for every committed
change, cheaply and mechanically; a codechecker does it
once for a submitted manuscript, expensively and with
judgment. In both cases the value comes from the same
property. The analysis runs somewhere that carries none
of the author's undeclared state, so anything the author
depended on without knowing it is exposed.

**What a human codechecker catches that the author's own
CI cannot.** The class of failure in which the CI
configuration itself encodes the author's assumptions. CI
is written by the author, so it tests what the author
thought to test, in an environment the author specified,
against outputs the author chose to compare. Consider a
workflow that installs a system library the Dockerfile
omits, or that silently skips the expensive analysis and
checks only the cheap one. Consider also one that
compares against a baseline the author generated after
the bug was introduced. Each passes indefinitely while
the compendium is not reproducible at all.

A codechecker reads the paper, forms an independent view
of what the analysis is supposed to produce, and checks
that the artifacts produce it. That is a judgment about
whether the right thing was verified. No amount of
automation supplies it, because the automation is the
thing in question.

The compact statement: CI answers 'does the analysis still
do what it did', and a codechecker answers 'does the
analysis do what the paper says'.
:::

## Exercise 8

A CI runner tests only what is checked out from version
control, which is exactly what is committed, no more. An
uncommitted change exists solely on the author's own
machine, so from the runner's point of view it does not
exist at all. The runner cannot fail on a problem it never
sees, and it cannot confirm a fix that was never pushed
either. 'Commit before you compute' is therefore what
makes CI's test meaningful in the first place. Without
it, a green build certifies a state of the repository
that nobody's actual analysis ran against.

**A concrete example.** An analyst fixes a bug in
`analysis/scripts/02_model.R`, reruns the report locally,
confirms the figure now looks right, and pushes. However,
the analyst forgets to `git add` a second file, a helper
function in `R/model_utils.R` the fix also depended on.
Locally, everything passes, because the uncommitted
helper is still on disk. On push, the runner checks out
only what was committed, and the helper function is
missing or stale. The render gate fails at the first
chunk that calls it. The author cannot reproduce this
failure by looking at their own unchanged working
directory until they notice the file was never staged.
:::

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-ci}

| Command or rule | What it does |
|---|---|
| `error-on: '"warning"'` (GitHub) / `error_on = "warning"` (`rcmdcheck`) | Fails `R CMD check` on any WARNING, including an undeclared import; `"error"` lets it through. |
| `zzrenvcheck::check_packages(strict = TRUE, error_on_fail = TRUE)` | Dependency-manifest gate; passing `error_on_fail = TRUE` explicitly keeps the step's failure from depending on how R was started. |
| `uses: actions/checkout@<full SHA> # v7.0.1` | Pins an action to a commit; Dependabot or Renovate can propose updates as pull requests. |
| `renv::dependencies('analysis')` | Scans source for packages actually used; the core of a hand-written dependency gate. |
| `rmarkdown::render(...)` in a CI step | The render gate: fails the job if any chunk errors on a clean restore. |
| `docker build -t compendium:ci .` | Rebuilds the project image from a clean machine, the L2 rebuild `zzc verify --full` requires. |
| `test-baseline-*.R` naming | What `zzc verify --full` and `ci/run-tests.R` look for to certify L3. |
| `digest(file = path, algo = 'sha256')` | Checksums a file's bytes that should not change (raw data); the wrong tool for a floating-point estimate. |
| `.Rbuildignore` entry for `analysis/` | Why `R CMD check` never sees analysis scripts or their dependencies. |
| Rule of thumb | Verify computational outputs within a tolerance; never hash rendered PDF or HTML bytes. |
| Habit 4 | Make every gate able to fail, and watch it fail once. |
| Habit 6 | Rebuild from clean, on a machine that is not yours. |

## Further reading

The distinction between capturing reproducibility and
validating it organizes this chapter. It is drawn out
across the introduction of this book (@sec-intro), and it
rests on the general framing of computational
reproducibility as a spectrum in @peng2011.

On independent, external verification, the CODECHECK
initiative described by Nust and Eglen
[@nust2021codecheck] is the most concrete model of
re-execution during peer review. It merits reading for
its account of what a codechecker does and does not
certify. The ACM's artifact review and badging policy
[@acm2020] documents the badge scheme now common at
computing venues.

On the persistence of the problem that all this machinery
addresses, Stodden and colleagues [@stodden2018] analyze
the effectiveness of journal reproducibility policies.
They find, soberingly, that a policy on paper is not a
reproduction in practice. Trisovic and colleagues
[@trisovic2022], in re-running thousands of deposited R
files, quantify how often re-execution simply fails,
which is the empirical case for the standing checks this
chapter describes.

For the practices that surround the tooling, the ten simple
rules of Sandve and colleagues [@sandve2013] place
automated checking and independent re-execution among their
recommendations. They also connect the mechanics of CI to
the habits that make it worthwhile.
